blocks.text: A central venous catheter (CVC) is a long, flexible catheter inserted into a large central vein, with its tip positioned in the central venous circulation, usually in the lower superior vena cava or at the cavoatrial junction, depending on the catheter type and intended use.

It provides reliable vascular access for administering medications, fluids, blood products and parenteral nutrition. It may also be used for central venous pressure monitoring, haemodialysis with a suitable catheter, and other specialised procedures.
Common insertion sites include the internal jugular, subclavian and femoral veins.
OSCE identification statement:

“This is a central venous catheter, used to obtain access to the central venous circulation for medication and fluid administration, blood sampling, haemodynamic monitoring and other specialised indications. It may be single-lumen, double-lumen or triple-lumen, depending on the intended use.”

blocks.text: These are different catheter designs within the broader category of central venous access devices. A PICC is central access despite being inserted through a peripheral vein.

items.text: Material: Commonly polyurethane or silicone, depending on catheter type.
Flexibility: Flexible enough to follow the venous pathway while maintaining lumen patency.
Radiopacity: Many catheters contain radiopaque material to aid identification on imaging.
Lumens: One or more independent channels.
Length and diameter: Depend on insertion site, patient size and intended application.
Sterility: Supplied sterile; many short-term catheters are single-use.
Connectors: Designed for compatible syringes and infusion systems.
Tip design: Varies according to intended use, including standard infusion, dialysis and specialised applications.
Fixation: May use sutures, a securement device, a dressing or a combination.

blocks.text: Safety point: Guidewire control is critical. Never release control of the wire, and never force a wire or catheter against resistance. CVC insertion is an invasive procedure that requires appropriate training, monitoring and local protocols.

blocks.text: A. Pneumothorax
Air enters the pleural space, especially with subclavian or certain internal jugular approaches. It may cause chest pain, breathlessness and reduced oxygen saturation.
B. Arterial puncture or injury
Accidental puncture of the carotid or subclavian artery may cause bleeding, haematoma or serious vascular injury.
C. Catheter-related bloodstream infection
Microorganisms may enter through the insertion site, hub or catheter. Prevention relies on aseptic insertion and meticulous maintenance.
D. Venous thrombosis
Thrombus can develop around the catheter, potentially causing swelling, pain or catheter dysfunction.
E. Malposition
The catheter tip may lie in an unintended vein or unsuitable position, causing poor function or other complications.
F. Other complications
Air embolism, arrhythmias during guidewire advancement, catheter occlusion, bleeding, vessel injury and rare catheter or guidewire fracture.

blocks.text: CVC insertion is sometimes necessary in emergencies, so many contraindications are relative rather than absolute.

items.text: Infection at the proposed insertion site.
Significant coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia.
Distorted anatomy or previous vascular surgery.
Existing thrombosis or obstruction of the intended vein.
Previous central venous devices or anatomical changes.
Severe respiratory compromise when a route with pneumothorax risk is being considered.
Patient factors that make safe positioning or procedural cooperation difficult.

blocks.text: The safest route and technique should be chosen after assessing urgency, anatomy, bleeding risk and available expertise.
A CVC may be connected to a pressure transducer to measure central venous pressure when clinically indicated.

CVP reflects pressure near the right atrium and is influenced by right atrial function, intrathoracic pressure, circulating volume, venous tone and mechanical ventilation.

rows: Early systolic change associated with tricuspid valve closure and bulging.
Atrial relaxation and downward movement of the tricuspid annulus during systole.
Right atrial filling while the tricuspid valve is closed.
Right atrial emptying into the right ventricle after the tricuspid valve opens.

items.text: Absent a waves: May occur in atrial fibrillation.
Prominent a waves: May occur with increased resistance to right ventricular filling.
Cannon a waves: May occur when atrial contraction occurs against a closed tricuspid valve, as in certain atrioventricular dissociation rhythms.
Large v waves: May occur in significant tricuspid regurgitation.
Raised mean CVP: May occur with right ventricular failure, tamponade, fluid overload or elevated intrathoracic pressure, among other causes.

blocks.text: Exam pearl: CVP must be interpreted alongside the patient's clinical state and other haemodynamic information. A single CVP value should not be used alone to decide whether a patient needs fluid resuscitation.

blocks.text: Q1. Identify this instrument.
This is a central venous catheter used for central vascular access, selected infusions, blood sampling and haemodynamic monitoring.
Q2. Name three common insertion sites.
Internal jugular, subclavian and femoral veins.
Q3. What is the Seldinger technique?
A method of vascular access in which a guidewire is introduced through a needle into the vessel, followed by passage of a dilator or catheter over the wire as appropriate.
Q4. What is the major immediate complication associated with subclavian access?
Pneumothorax is an important immediate complication, although arterial injury and bleeding can also occur.
Q5. What are the major complications of a CVC?
Mechanical injury, arterial puncture, pneumothorax, malposition, bleeding, infection, thrombosis and catheter occlusion.
Q6. What is the purpose of a multi-lumen catheter?
It allows separate infusion pathways for compatible medications, fluids and selected sampling or monitoring tasks.
Q7. What is a PICC?
A peripherally inserted central catheter, introduced through a peripheral vein with its tip advanced into the central venous circulation.
Q8. How do you prevent catheter-related infection?
Appropriate hand hygiene, maximal sterile barrier precautions during insertion, proper skin antisepsis, aseptic hub access, appropriate dressing care and prompt removal when unnecessary.
Q9. What should be done if arterial placement of a large-bore dilator or catheter is suspected?
Do not simply pull it out. Leave it in place, avoid further manipulation and obtain urgent specialist vascular or interventional advice.
